lead: The sinc pulse meets Nyquist's zero-ISI condition in the least bandwidth, but its rectangular spectrum cannot be built and its 1/t tails turn a small timing error into large ISI. The raised cosine pulse rounds the corners of that rectangle with a cosine roll-off set by one number, the roll-off factor α between 0 and 1. It spends a known extra bandwidth and gets tails that die as 1/t³. The eye pattern is the oscilloscope picture that shows whether the shaped pulses are still clean where the sampler fires.
prereq: You need: ISI and the Nyquist criterion (the Nyquist bandwidth Rs/2).

sections.h3: From a brick wall to a cosine roll-off

blocks.text: The criterion asks that the copies of P(f), spaced 1/T apart, add up to a constant. A rectangle does this, but so does any spectrum whose fall around R<sub>s</sub>/2 is odd-symmetric: what one copy loses just below R<sub>s</sub>/2, the next copy adds back just above it. The raised cosine spectrum uses half a cosine for that fall. It is flat from 0 to (1 − α)R<sub>s</sub>/2, then falls smoothly to zero at (1 + α)R<sub>s</sub>/2.
Here B is the baseband bandwidth in hertz, Rs = 1/T is the symbol rate in baud and α is the roll-off factor, 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.
Here α is the excess as a fraction of the Nyquist bandwidth: α = 0.25 spends 25 % more than R<sub>s</sub>/2.

α = 0 is the sinc with B = R<sub>s</sub>/2. α = 1 doubles the band to B = R<sub>s</sub> and gives the gentlest filter. Real links sit between, typically α = 0.2 to 0.5. Read the other way, a channel of bandwidth B carries at most R<sub>s</sub> = 2B/(1 + α) symbols per second.

sections.h3: The pulse in time, and the root raised cosine pair

blocks.text: Here sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx), so p(0) = 1. The sinc factor keeps every zero at t = nT, which keeps zero ISI. The second factor makes the tails fall as 1/t³ instead of 1/t.

Where the bracket is zero, at t = ±T/(2α), the formula reads 0/0 and the limit is p = (π/4)·sinc(1/(2α)). For α = 0.5 that point is t = T, where p is zero anyway; for α = 0.35 it is t = 1.43T, where p = −0.171.

The tails decide practical success. Halfway between instants, at t = 2.5T, the sinc is still 0.127, the raised cosine with α = 0.25 is 0.087, with α = 0.5 only 0.017, and with α = 1 exactly zero. Small tails mean a late sample picks up little from the neighbours.

The receive filter also has a second job: it should be matched to the incoming pulse to give the best signal-to-noise ratio (see the matched filter). Both demands are met by splitting the spectrum: a root raised cosine (RRC) filter, with |G(f)| = √P(f), at the transmitter and the same RRC at the receiver. Their cascade is the raised cosine, so the sampler sees zero ISI and a matched filter at once. One RRC alone does not give zero ISI; only the pair does.

The eye pattern (eye diagram) is made by feeding the receive-filter output to an oscilloscope triggered by the symbol clock, with a sweep of about two symbol periods. Thousands of random symbol sequences pile up on the screen, and for binary data the traces leave an open space shaped like an eye. Figure 5.2.1 shows the eye of the worked example's α = 0.5 pulse.

items: Vertical opening at the sampling instant: the distance between the lowest +1 trace and the highest −1 trace. It is the noise margin. ISI shrinks it.
Horizontal opening: the range of sampling instants over which the eye is still open. It is the tolerance to timing error and jitter.
Slope of the traces near the sampling instant: a steep slope means the opening shrinks fast when the clock is off, so the system is sensitive to timing error.
Spread of the zero crossings: their width is the timing jitter that the clock recovery circuit sees.

blocks.text: Sample in the middle of the eye, where the vertical opening is largest. For the α = 0.5 pulse, binary data and every possible neighbour pattern, the worst +1 sample is 1 at the centre, 0.785 at 0.1T off and 0.535 at 0.2T off. For α = 0.25 the same offsets give 0.652 and 0.289: less bandwidth buys a narrower eye. A channel that cuts high frequencies, a wrong α or a badly placed clock all show up as a closing eye.

examples.question: A binary baseband link carries 4800 bit/s through a raised cosine system with α = 0.5. Find the symbol rate, the symbol period, the Nyquist bandwidth, the transmission bandwidth and the excess bandwidth. What would α = 0 and α = 1 need?
steps: Binary: one bit per symbol, so R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub> = 4800 baud.
Excess = B − 2400 = 1200 Hz. Check: αR<sub>s</sub>/2 = 0.5 × 2400 = 1200 Hz.
α = 0: B = 2400 Hz, but the filter is the unbuildable brick wall. α = 1: B = 2400 × 2 = 4800 Hz, 1200 Hz more than α = 0.5.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 4800 baud, T = 208.3 µs, Nyquist bandwidth 2400 Hz, B = 3600 Hz, excess 1200 Hz; α = 0 needs 2400 Hz and α = 1 needs 4800 Hz.

examples.question: A cable passes 0 to 3600 Hz. (a) What is the highest binary bit rate with α = 0.2? (b) The link must carry 9600 bit/s. Can binary do it? If 4-level PAM is used, what is the largest α allowed?
steps: (a) R<sub>s</sub> = 2B/(1 + α) = 2 × 3600/1.2 = 6000 baud. Binary gives R<sub>b</sub> = 6000 bit/s.
(b) Binary at 9600 bit/s means R<sub>s</sub> = 9600 baud, which needs at least R<sub>s</sub>/2 = 4800 Hz even with α = 0. 4800 Hz > 3600 Hz, so binary cannot do it.
4-PAM carries 2 bits per symbol: R<sub>s</sub> = 9600/2 = 4800 baud, Nyquist bandwidth 2400 Hz.
examples.answer: (a) 6000 bit/s; (b) binary would need at least 4800 Hz, so no; 4-PAM at 4800 baud fits with α up to 0.5.

traps: Dropping the half: writing B = R<sub>s</sub>(1 + α) or excess = αR<sub>s</sub>. The correct forms are B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α) and excess = αR<sub>s</sub>/2.
Putting the bit rate where the symbol rate belongs. For M-PAM use R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/log₂M in the bandwidth formula.
Choosing α = 0 because it is the narrowest. The brick wall cannot be built and its eye closes under the smallest timing error; justify a practical α of 0.2 to 0.5.
Expecting one root raised cosine filter to give zero ISI. Only the transmit and receive RRC filters in cascade make the raised cosine.

quiz.q: Define the roll-off factor α and give its range.
quiz.a: α is the excess bandwidth of a raised cosine spectrum as a fraction of the Nyquist bandwidth R<sub>s</sub>/2, so B = (R<sub>s</sub>/2)(1 + α). Its range is 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.

quiz.q: What does the horizontal opening of an eye pattern measure?
quiz.a: The range of sampling instants over which the eye stays open: the tolerance of the receiver to timing error and jitter.

quiz.q: Why is the raised cosine preferred to the sinc although it needs more bandwidth?
quiz.a: Its spectrum has a gradual edge that real filters can approach, and its tails fall as 1/t³, so a timing error picks up little ISI. The sinc's brick-wall spectrum cannot be built and its 1/t tails add up under a timing error.

quiz.q: A raised cosine system runs at 2400 baud with α = 0.35. Find the bandwidth and the excess bandwidth.
A binary link sends 9600 bit/s with α = 0.25. Find T, the Nyquist bandwidth and the transmission bandwidth.
quiz.a: R<sub>s</sub> = 9600 baud, T = 104.2 µs, Nyquist bandwidth 4800 Hz, B = 4800 × 1.25 = 6000 Hz.

quiz.q: An eye pattern has a wide horizontal opening but a small vertical opening at the centre. What is the likely cause?
quiz.a: The timing is fine, since the eye is open over a wide range of instants. The small vertical opening points to amplitude trouble at the sampling instant: additive noise, or residual ISI from a channel that does not give the zeros at nT. An equalizer helps the ISI; more signal power helps the noise.

quiz.q: Why does a link use two root raised cosine filters instead of one raised cosine filter at the transmitter?
quiz.a: The overall pulse must be a raised cosine for zero ISI, and the receive filter must be matched to the incoming pulse for the best SNR. With an RRC at each end both hold: the receive RRC is matched to the transmit RRC, and their product is the raised cosine. A raised cosine at the transmitter alone leaves the receive filter free to be either wide (more noise) or narrow (more ISI).

beyond: Broadcast and satellite standards offer a short menu of roll-off factors so operators can trade bandwidth against out-of-band emission; DVB-S2 is a good example to read about. Very high-speed copper and optical links push α low and repair the rest with equalizers. Search for root raised cosine filter design and eye mask testing.

figure.caption: Left: the raised cosine spectra of the 4800 baud example. α = 0.5 needs 3600 Hz, between the 2400 Hz brick wall and the 4800 Hz of α = 1. Right: the α = 0.5 eye for binary data. At the centre every trace passes through ±1; 0.1T away the worst +1 trace has fallen to 0.785.

spec.aria: Left, three spectra: a rectangle to 2400 hertz, a cosine roll-off ending at 3600 hertz and one ending at 4800 hertz. Right, an eye diagram of all data patterns: wide open at the sampling instant with opening 2, and worst sample 0.785 at a tenth of a symbol period away.
